title: Routing and App Structure
summary: Turn one HTML page into many with React Router 8: routes, layouts, params, loaders and actions, and a folder structure that grows with the app.
intro: A shop has many screens: the product list, a product page, the cart, a login page, an account page. People expect each one to have its own address, one they can bookmark, send to a friend, and come back to with the Back button. But your Vite React app is a single HTML page. Routing is how one page shows many screens, each at its own address. This lesson uses React Router 8: how a single-page app fakes pages and what that costs, routes and nested layouts, reading the address, loading data before a page shows, sending forms, handling errors and logged-out visitors, and arranging your files so the app still makes sense as it grows.

steps.title: How a single-page app fakes pages
steps.body:
The first time you put a React app online, there's a fair chance that a link someone shares opens a 404 page instead of the product it points to. That bug, and most of how routing works, makes sense once you see the trick a single-page app plays on the browser.

## Pages the old way

On a site made of HTML files, every page is its own document, as the web course showed. Click a link, and the browser asks the server for the new address, throws away the page it was showing, along with everything its JavaScript held, and draws the new document from the top. Even a header that's the same on both pages is downloaded and drawn again.

## One page that changes

A **single-page app**, or SPA, works differently. The server sends one `index.html` and the JavaScript bundle once, and from then on, JavaScript draws every screen. Your Vite React app is one: a single `index.html` with an empty `<div id="root">`.

To make that one page feel like many, the app needs a **router**: code that reads the address and decides which components to render for it. Each pairing of an address pattern with what to show is a **route**, like `/products/:slug` showing a product page. Changing screens without asking the server for a new document is called **client-side routing**, and it takes three moves:

1. You click a link the router made. The router calls `preventDefault()` on the click, so the browser doesn't load anything.
2. The router calls `history.pushState()`, the History API from the web course, which changes the address and adds an entry to the history, again with no request.
3. The router renders the components that match the new address. React's commit changes only what differs, so the header stays put and only the middle of the page changes.

```diagram routing-and-structure-spa
A click changes the address and swaps one component. No request for HTML goes out.
```

Back and Forward work too. The browser fires a `popstate` event, the router reads the address it moved to, and renders that screen.

## What you gain

Moving between screens is fast, since at most some data travels, never a whole document. Everything outside the part that changes keeps running: an open cart drawer, a playing video, a half-typed search. And state in memory survives from one screen to the next.

## What you trade

- **The first visit waits for JavaScript.** Until the bundle loads and runs, the page is empty. That's client-side rendering, from the Where HTML Is Made lesson, and search engines or link previews that don't run JavaScript see only that empty shell.
- **The server must answer every address with index.html.** Someone opens a shared link to `/products/hip-pack-5`. No file has that path, so a plain static server answers 404 before your router even loads. The fix is a **fallback** rule: for any path that isn't a real file, send `index.html`. Vite's dev server and `npm run preview` do it for you, as the example shows. Your host needs it too, and every host has a setting for it, like this line in the config of nginx, a popular web server:

```text
try_files $uri /index.html;
```

- **What the browser did for free is now your app's job.** That means the title in the tab, a page-not-found screen, and the scroll position when you go back. The router helps with all three, and the next part shows how.

Despite those costs, an SPA is the right shape for apps people use for a while, like a shop, a dashboard, or an inbox. Pages that must show their content the moment they load, for search engines above all, are better made on the server, which the Next.js course covers.

examples.title: A deep link on the dev server
examples.prompt: With `npm run dev` running, ask the dev server for a product's address from a second terminal, the way a shared link would.
examples.explanation:
There's no file at `products/hip-pack-5` in your project, yet the answer starts with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` and `Content-Type: text/html`, and its body is your `index.html`: the same empty root div, and the same script tag for `/src/main.tsx`. In development Vite also adds two small scripts to the top of the head, for hot reloading, which a build doesn't have.

That's the fallback at work. A browser that got this answer would load the bundle, the router would read `/products/hip-pack-5`, and the product page would appear. After you deploy, run the same command against your real site. A 404 there means your host has no fallback rule yet, and every shared link to a page inside your app is broken.

steps.title: Routes, layouts, and links
steps.body:
Most screens in an app share a frame: the header with the logo and the cart, the navigation, the footer. Nested routes let you write that frame once and let the address decide what goes inside it. This part sets up React Router and builds the shop's routes.

## Installing React Router

React Router is the router most React apps use. Version 8 is one package:

```bash
npm install react-router
```

It has three modes, and this course uses **data mode**: you describe your routes as plain objects, which also lets a route load data before it renders, as part 4 shows. Everything comes from `react-router`, except `RouterProvider`, which renders the router into the page and comes from `react-router/dom`. Older guides import from `react-router-dom`, a package version 8 no longer has.

## Route objects

`createBrowserRouter` takes a list of route objects. The first example is the shop's. Each object can have:

- `path`, the address pattern, like `"cart"`. A segment starting with a colon, like `":slug"`, matches any value, which the next part reads.
- `Component`, what to render when the route matches.
- `children`, routes nested inside this one, whose paths add on to the parent's: `":slug"` inside `"products"` matches `/products/ridge-2p-tent`.
- `index: true` instead of a path, for the child that shows at the parent's own address, like the list at `/products`.

Create the router once, at the top level of its own file, and never inside a component, so it isn't rebuilt on every render.

## Nested routes and the Outlet

For `/products/ridge-2p-tent`, the router finds a chain of routes, from the outside in: the root route at `/`, then `products`, then `:slug`. It renders the outermost route's component, `RootLayout`, and wherever that component puts an `<Outlet />`, it renders the next route in the chain. A route with a `Component` and `children`, like the root here, is called a **layout route**. The `products` route has a path but no component, so it only groups the two routes under it.

```diagram routing-and-structure-nested
The address picks a chain of routes. Each one renders inside its parent's Outlet.
```

When you click from one product to another, only the part inside the `Outlet` changes. The header and footer stay mounted, with their state.

## Links

`<Link to="/cart">` renders an ordinary `<a href="/cart">`, so opening it in a new tab, copying its address, and screen readers all work. A normal click on it, though, is handled by the router, without a request. A plain `<a href>` to a page in your own app would reload the whole page, so use `Link` for those, and `<a>` only for other sites.

`NavLink` is a `Link` that knows when it matches the current address. It then gets an `active` class for your CSS, and the attribute `aria-current="page"`, which screen readers announce as current page. A `NavLink` matches its own path and every path under it, so Shop stays highlighted on a product page. Add `end` to match the exact path only, as the logo's link to `/` does, since every address starts with `/`.

## A page for wrong addresses

In an SPA the server answers every address with `index.html` and a 200, so the server's own 404 page never shows. A route with `path: "*"` matches any address no other route matched, and its component is your not-found page.

## A title for every page

Every address loads the same `index.html`, so the tab shows its one title until you set another. In React 19, any component can render a `<title>` or a `<meta>` tag, and React moves it into the document's head, then removes it when the component goes away. So give each page component its own: `<title>Cart · Trailhead</title>`. A title must be one string, so when it holds a value, build it with a template literal:

```tsx
<title>{`${product.name} · Trailhead`}</title>
```

There's a limit: these tags only appear once JavaScript runs. A search engine or a chat app's link preview that reads only the HTML sees the title in `index.html`, the problem the Where HTML Is Made lesson described. When that matters, render the page on the server.

Last, the scroll position. Put `<ScrollRestoration />` once in your root layout, and the router does what the browser did for documents: a new page starts at the top, and Back returns you to where you were.

examples.title: The shop's routes
examples.prompt: `src/app/router.tsx`, the first version: a layout for the whole app, a home page, the product list and product pages, the cart, and a page for any other address. Later parts add more to it.
examples.explanation:
The root route has the path `/` and the `RootLayout` component, so every page renders inside it. Its children are the pages. The home page is the index route, shown at `/` itself. The `products` route only groups its two children, so `/products` shows `ProductsPage` and `/products/trail-pack-45` shows `ProductPage`. The `*` route comes last in the list, but order doesn't decide the match: the router ranks routes by how specific they are, so a real path always beats `*`.

The page components come from their features' folders, like `@/features/products`. Part 6 explains that layout.

examples.title: The layout with an Outlet
examples.prompt: `src/app/RootLayout.tsx`: the header, the footer, and an `Outlet` where each page goes.
examples.code:
import { NavLink, Outlet, ScrollRestoration } from "react-router";

export function RootLayout() {
  return (
    <>
      <header className="site-header">
        <NavLink to="/" end className="logo">
          Trailhead
        </NavLink>
        <nav aria-label="Main">
          <NavLink to="/products">Shop</NavLink>
          <NavLink to="/cart">Cart</NavLink>
        </nav>
      </header>
      <main>
        <Outlet />
      </main>
      <footer className="site-footer">Free shipping on orders over $50</footer>
      <ScrollRestoration />
    </>
  );
}
examples.explanation: Everything in this component shows on every page. The `Outlet` in `main` is where the router puts the matching child route, the product list or the cart. The logo's `NavLink` has `end`, so it's only active at `/` itself. Without `end` it would match every address, since they all start with `/`. On the product list, the Shop link gets `class="active"` and `aria-current="page"`, and so it does on every product page under `/products`. `ScrollRestoration` renders nothing visible.

examples.title: Handing the router to React
examples.prompt: `src/main.tsx` renders `RouterProvider` with the router, in place of the `App` component the template started with.
examples.explanation: `RouterProvider` comes from `react-router/dom`, the one import in React Router that does. It listens to the History API, matches the address against your routes, and renders the chain of matching components, starting with `RootLayout`. `App.tsx` from the template has no job anymore: what it used to show is now the home page route. StrictMode still wraps everything, as it did before.

steps.title: Reading the URL: params and search params
steps.body:
The address is state the browser keeps for you. It survives a reload, it can be bookmarked or sent to a friend, and Back and Forward move through it. So what a screen shows, like which product and which filters, belongs in the address, and the Sharing State lesson called this **URL state**. This part reads it and writes it.

## Params: the parts of the path

A route's dynamic segment, like `:slug` in `/products/:slug`, is a **param**. `useParams` returns them as an object:

```tsx sketch
const { slug } = useParams();
// at /products/ridge-2p-tent, slug is "ridge-2p-tent"
```

TypeScript types every param as `string | undefined`, since a component can't know which route rendered it. Your route guarantees the value here, but the type doesn't, so handle the `undefined`, like `params.slug ?? ""`. In part 4, a loader reads the same `params` before the page renders, which is where most pages use them.

## Search params: the query string

Filters, a search, a sort order, a page number: these go in the query string, like `/products?category=tents&page=2`. `useSearchParams` gives you the current query as a `URLSearchParams`, the object from the web course, and a function to set a new one:

```tsx sketch
const [searchParams, setSearchParams] = useSearchParams();
const category = searchParams.get("category") ?? "";
```

Setting search params navigates: the address changes, a history entry is added, and every component that reads them renders with the new values. Back then undoes the last filter, the way people expect. For changes that shouldn't stack up in the history, like each letter typed in a box, pass `{ replace: true }` as the second argument.

Keeping filters here, rather than in `useState`, gives you more than shareable links. There's one copy of the truth, so nothing has to be kept in sync: the address is the state, and the list, the dropdown, and the page count all read it. Everything in it is a string, though. `searchParams.get("page")` is `"2"`, not `2`, or `null` when it's missing, so convert it and check it, since anyone can type anything into an address. The next lesson shows a neat way to check values like these.

## A form that writes the address

React Router's `<Form>` component with no `method` works like an HTML form sent with GET, as the web course showed: it turns its fields into a query string and goes to that address, but without reloading the page. A search box needs nothing else, no state and no handler, as the example shows.

## Navigating from code

`useNavigate` returns a function that goes somewhere when your code decides to: `navigate("/cart")`, `navigate(-1)` to go back one step, or `navigate("/", { replace: true })` to replace the current history entry. React Router's own advice is to reach for it last. Use a `Link` when someone clicks to go somewhere, since it's a real link that can open in a new tab. Use a `<Form>` for a search, and `redirect` in a loader or an action, both in the next part, when the move follows data. Keep `useNavigate` for moves nobody clicked, like logging someone out after an hour without activity.

examples.title: Filters that live in the address
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/ProductFilters.tsx`: a search box and a category dropdown above the product list, both reading and writing the query string.
examples.explanation:
Both controls read their values from the address, so a link to `/products?category=tents&q=dome` opens with Tents chosen and dome in the box.

Choosing a category calls `setSearchParams` with a function, like an updater function for state. It gets the current params, sets or deletes `category`, and also deletes `page`, since page 3 of all products means nothing for tents. `q` stays as it was, since the function only changes what it touches. Then the router goes to the new address, and the list renders for it.

The search box is a `<Form>`. Pressing Enter in it goes to `/products?q=` plus what you typed, with no handler. A GET form sends only its own fields, so a hidden input carries the current category along, or a search would drop the filter. The input uses `defaultValue`, the uncontrolled kind from the State and Events lesson, since the address, not React state, holds the submitted value.

steps.title: Loaders and actions
steps.body:
The Effects, Refs, and Browser APIs lesson warned that fetching data in an effect has traps. One of them is order. A page that fetches in an effect renders empty first, then starts its request, then renders again with the data. If a component inside it fetches the same way, its request starts only after the first one finishes. Each step waits for the last, a chain called a **waterfall**. Loaders fix the order.

## Where the data comes from

From here on, the shop gets its data from the Trailhead API, the course's backend from the first lesson: a small Node.js server in one file, with nothing to install. To get it, [add the Trailhead API to your Playground](/playground?add=trailhead-api). That makes a `trailhead-api` folder at the Playground's top level, next to your `trailhead` project, holding the server, `server.mjs`, the description of every request it takes, `openapi.yaml`, the shop's product photos in `images/`, and a `README.md`.

The API names each product's photo by a path like `/images/products/trail-pack-45.webp`, and the browser asks your shop for it, not the API. So copy the photos into the shop's `public` folder once, from the Playground folder:

```bash
cp -r trailhead-api/images trailhead/public/
```

Start the API in a second terminal, from the Playground folder, and leave it running while you work:

```bash
node trailhead-api/server.mjs
```

It prints one line, Trailhead API on http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1, and waits for requests. Every path it answers starts with `/v1`, like `/v1/products`. It keeps everything in memory, so each start begins from the same twelve products and two accounts you can log in as, `sam@example.com` and `ana@example.com`, both with the password `trailhead`, and stopping it with Ctrl+C throws away whatever you changed. Start it as `TRAILHEAD_DELAYS=1 node trailhead-api/server.mjs` instead, and it answers a little slowly, like a real network, so you can see your loading states.

The app asks for those paths on its own origin, and Vite passes them on to the API, with the dev proxy you met in the web course. That's the `/v1` in `.env` from Starting a New React Project. Add the proxy to `vite.config.ts`, for the dev server and for `npm run preview`:

```ts sketch
server: { proxy: { "/v1": "http://127.0.0.1:4000" } },
preview: { proxy: { "/v1": "http://127.0.0.1:4000" } },
```

To the browser, the page and the API now share one origin, so the cookies the API sets come back with every request, and there's no CORS to set up.

## Loaders

A **loader** is a function on a route that gets the route's data. The router calls it as soon as a navigation to that route starts, before anything renders, and it calls the loaders of every route in the chain at the same time. When they've all finished, it renders the new page with the data already there.

```diagram routing-and-structure-loaders
Effects start each request after a render. Loaders start them all when you click.
```

The first example holds the shop's two loaders. A loader receives the route's `params` and the `request`, a standard `Request` object with the full address in `request.url` and a `request.signal` that aborts if you navigate somewhere else before it finishes, which you pass on to `fetch`. Whatever it returns, the page reads with `useLoaderData`:

```tsx sketch
const product = useLoaderData<typeof productLoader>();
```

`typeof productLoader` hands TypeScript the loader's type, so `product` is typed as whatever the loader returns. Put loaders in their own file, not in a component's file: your project's lint rule `react/only-export-components` warns about files that export anything besides components, because the dev server can't swap those in place when you save.

On the very first page load, there's nothing to show until the loaders finish. A `HydrateFallback` component on the root route renders meanwhile, a small spinner or the page's empty frame. Leave it out and the console warns about it.

These loaders trust the server's JSON with `as`, a type assertion, which tells TypeScript the type without checking it. The next lesson replaces that with a real check, and adds a cache, so going back to a page you've seen doesn't fetch it again.

## Pending pages

While a navigation's loaders run, the old page stays on the screen, which can make a slow click feel broken. `useNavigation` tells you what the router is doing: its `state` is `"loading"` while loaders run, `"submitting"` while an action runs, and `"idle"` otherwise. The root layout can show a progress bar:

```tsx sketch
const navigation = useNavigation();
// ...
{navigation.state === "loading" && <div className="progress-bar" role="progressbar" aria-label="Loading page" />}
```

## Actions

Changing data has its own function. An **action** is a function on a route that handles a form sent to it. React Router's `<Form method="post">` doesn't send the form to a server. It calls the action of its route with the form's fields in `request.formData()`, the same `FormData` you met in the web course. The action calls your API, then either returns data, which the page reads with `useActionData`, or returns `redirect("/somewhere")` to go to another page.

After an action finishes, the router runs the loaders of the routes on screen again, which is called **revalidation**. The page shows fresh data without any code of yours, like a cart count that changes after you add an item. For a form that shouldn't change the page at all, like an Add to cart button on every card, `useFetcher` gives you a `<fetcher.Form>` that calls an action without navigating.

The second and third examples are the login page: an action that posts to the API, and the form that calls it. Add the route with both, `{ path: "login", Component: LoginPage, action: loginAction }`. The Forms and Actions in React lesson later in this section builds more forms, with React's own form tools.

examples.title: Loaders for the product pages
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/loaders.ts`. In `router.tsx`, the list route gets `loader: productsLoader` and the product route gets `loader: productLoader`.
examples.explanation:
`productsLoader` passes the query string straight through: `/products?category=tents` asks the API for `/v1/products?category=tents`. So the filters from the previous part need no code of their own. Changing the address runs the loader again.

`productLoader` reads `params.slug` and asks for that one product. Each error goes its own way. A 404 is expected, since anyone can type a wrong address, so it throws `data(...)` with a message and the status, which React Router delivers to an error page as a proper response. Any other failure throws an ordinary `Error`. Throwing, not returning, means the page component only ever renders with a real product, and part 5 shows where thrown errors land.

`encodeURIComponent` keeps a strange slug from changing the shape of the API address.

examples.title: The login action
examples.prompt: `src/features/auth/loginAction.ts` sends the email and password to the Trailhead API's `POST /v1/auth/login`, which answers with a session cookie or a 401.
examples.explanation:
The action reads the two fields from the form and sends them as JSON. The API is on the same origin, through Vite's proxy, so the browser stores the `th_session` cookie it sets and sends it with every later request, as cookies do.

A 401 isn't a crash. It's a wrong password, so the action returns a message for the form to show. Success returns a `redirect`, to where the visitor was headed. That address comes from `?next=` in the URL, which part 5's guard adds. Because anyone can put anything in a URL, the action accepts only a path on this site, one starting with a single `/`, so a crafted link like `/login?next=https://evil.example` can't send people to another site after they log in.

examples.title: The login form
examples.prompt: `src/features/auth/LoginPage.tsx`, the component on the `login` route. Its `Form` posts to that route's action.
examples.explanation:
`<Form method="post">` gathers the fields by their `name`, `email` and `password`, and calls `loginAction`. While it runs, `navigation.state` is `"submitting"`, so the button turns off and says Logging in…, and a double click can't send the form twice.

When the action returns `{ error }`, `useActionData` hands it back here and the message shows. Its `role="alert"` makes screen readers announce it. When the action redirects instead, this page goes away. The `required` attributes and the `type="email"` are the browser's own checks from the web course, and they still run before the action is called.

steps.title: Errors, lazy routes, and guards
steps.body:
Three more things every real app needs. Something will go wrong, a missing product, a server that's down, a bug, and the app should say so instead of going blank. Some pages are for logged-in people only. And some pages are visited so rarely that their code shouldn't slow down everyone's first load.

## Error boundaries

When a component throws an error while rendering, React can't finish the tree, so it removes your whole app from the page, and the visitor sees a blank screen. An **error boundary** stops that: a component that catches errors thrown in the part of the tree below it and shows a fallback in place of that part.

In React Router, every route can have an `ErrorBoundary` component. An error thrown in a route's loader, its action, or its component renders the closest `ErrorBoundary` at or above that route, in place of the route, so the layouts around it keep working. Inside it, `useRouteError()` returns what was thrown, and `isRouteErrorResponse(error)` tells you whether it was a response thrown on purpose with `data(...)`, which has a `status`, or an unexpected error.

Put one on the root route to catch everything, and closer ones where a page can say something more useful:

```tsx sketch
{
  path: "/",
  Component: RootLayout,
  ErrorBoundary: RootErrorBoundary,
  HydrateFallback: PageSpinner,
  children: [
    // ...
    { path: ":slug", Component: ProductPage, loader: productLoader, ErrorBoundary: ProductErrorBoundary },
  ],
}
```

## Lazy routes

The Re-rendering and Performance lesson used `lazy` to split off a component's code. A route can do the same with its `lazy` property: give each piece of the route a function that imports it, and the route's code becomes its own chunk, loaded the first time someone navigates there.

```tsx sketch
{
  path: "account",
  middleware: [requireUser],
  lazy: {
    loader: async () => (await import("@/features/auth/accountLoader")).accountLoader,
    Component: async () => (await import("@/features/auth/AccountPage")).AccountPage,
  },
}
```

The router loads the chunk as part of the navigation, at the same time as the data, and shows the page when both arrive, so you need no `Suspense` here. Split off pages most visitors never open, like an account page or an admin screen, and keep the pages everyone sees in the main bundle. The third example shows the chunks in a build.

## Guards with middleware

That route also has `middleware`: a list of functions the router runs before the route's loaders and actions, on every navigation to it or to a route inside it. A **guard** is middleware that decides whether you may see a page at all. `requireUser`, the second example, asks the API who's logged in. When the answer is 401, it throws a `redirect` to the login page, with the current address in `?next=` so the login action can send you back.

When you are logged in, the guard passes the user along to the loaders through the router's **context**, an object every middleware, loader, and action in one navigation shares. It's made with React Router's own `createContext`, not React's:

```tsx sketch
export const userContext = createContext<User>();
// in a loader:
const user = context.get(userContext);
```

A guard in the browser is there for the visitor, not for security. Anyone can change the JavaScript running in their own browser and skip it. What keeps an account private is the API, which checks the session cookie on every request and answers 401 without it, as Trailhead's does. The Web Vulnerabilities and Secrets lesson comes back to this.

examples.title: An error page for missing products
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/ProductErrorBoundary.tsx`, the `ErrorBoundary` of the product route. The root route's `RootErrorBoundary` handles everything else.
examples.explanation:
When `productLoader` throws `data("There's no product called nope.", { status: 404 })`, this component renders where the product page would have been, inside the layout, so the header and the Shop link still work. `error.data` is the message the loader threw.

Anything else, a 500 from the API or a bug, isn't something this page knows how to explain, so it throws the error again. Throwing in an error boundary passes the error up to the next one, the root's, which shows a general Something went wrong page and logs the error. A missing product gets a helpful message, and the rest still gets caught.

examples.title: A guard for logged-in pages
examples.prompt: `src/features/auth/requireUser.ts`. `userContext.ts`, next to it, makes the context with `createContext<User>()`.
examples.explanation:
`MiddlewareFunction` is React Router's type for middleware, so `request` and `context` come typed. The function asks `GET /v1/me` who's logged in, and the browser sends the session cookie along on its own.

A 401 means nobody is, so it throws a redirect, and the account page's loader never runs. `encodeURIComponent` keeps the `?` and `&` of the current address from breaking the new one: from `/account`, you land on `/login?next=%2Faccount`. Any other failure is a real error, for the error boundary. Otherwise it stores the user in the context, and `accountLoader` reads it with `context.get(userContext)`, with no second request.

Middleware can also run code after the route's loaders by calling the `next` function it receives. A guard has nothing to do afterwards, so it leaves `next` out, and the router calls it for you.

examples.title: The account page's own chunks
examples.prompt: Building the shop with the lazy `account` route.

steps.title: Organizing files as the app grows
steps.body:
With a dozen files, it hardly matters where each one goes. With a few hundred, where files go decides how fast you find things, how safely you can change one, and how often two people's work collides. Settle the layout early, while moving files is still cheap.

## By type or by feature

The first layout most projects try groups files **by type**: every component in `components/`, every hook in `hooks/`, every page in `pages/`, every API call in `api/`. It's tidy at first. But a change to the cart then touches four folders, and nothing tells you which components belong to the cart and which to checkout.

Grouping **by feature** keeps everything about one part of the app together: its pages, components, loaders, actions, and types. The shop's `src` folder looks like the diagram:

```diagram routing-and-structure-src
Imports flow one way: from app, to features, to the shared folders.
```

- `app/` is the wiring: the router, the root layout, the error pages, and later the providers. It's the only folder that knows about every feature.
- `features/` holds one folder per part of the app: `products`, `cart`, `auth`, `checkout`.
- `components/ui/` holds small building blocks any feature can use, like a button or the `PageSpinner`.
- `hooks/` holds custom hooks shared across features, and `lib/` holds plain helpers with no components, like `formatPrice`.

## A feature's public face

Each feature has an `index.ts` that re-exports what the rest of the app may use, as the first example shows. Everything not exported there is the feature's own business. Other code imports `@/features/products`, never a file inside it, so you can rename, split, or merge the feature's files without touching anything outside. Inside a feature, files import each other by relative path, like `./ProductCard`.

There's one deliberate exception. Lazy pages, like `AccountPage`, stay out of `index.ts`, and `router.tsx` imports them by their full path. Exporting them from `index.ts` would pull them into the main bundle, as the previous part's build showed.

## Imports go one way

The diagram's arrows are the rule: `app` may import from features, features from the shared folders, and never the other way. When two features need the same thing, it moves down into `components/ui` or `lib`, instead of one feature reaching into the other. Code that depends on less is easier to test and to change.

## Let the linter hold the line

Rules that live in people's heads get broken on a busy day. Your linter can check this one with `no-restricted-imports`, added to `.oxlintrc.json`:

```json
{
  "rules": {
    "no-restricted-imports": [
      "error",
      { "patterns": [{ "group": ["@/features/*/*"], "message": "Import from the feature's index.ts, like @/features/products." }] }
    ]
  },
  "overrides": [{ "files": ["src/app/router.tsx"], "rules": { "no-restricted-imports": "off" } }]
}
```

The pattern forbids any import that reaches inside a feature's folder. The override lets `router.tsx` alone do it, for its lazy imports. The second example shows what breaking the rule looks like.

## Tests next to the code

When you write tests, in the Testing lessons later in this course, put each one next to what it tests: `ProductCard.test.tsx` beside `ProductCard.tsx`. You'll see at a glance what's tested, and deleting a feature means deleting one folder, tests and all.

The loaders in this lesson call `fetch` directly and trust whatever comes back. The next lesson, Calling APIs From React, gives the shop one checked client for the Trailhead API, and a cache for what it returns.

examples.title: The products feature's public API
examples.prompt: `src/features/products/index.ts`: the only file the rest of the app imports from the products feature.
examples.explanation:
Four page components and two loaders are public, because `router.tsx` needs them, and so are two types other features use, like the cart showing a `ProductSummary`. `ProductCard` and `ProductFilters` aren't exported, so they're free to change.

`export type` re-exports a type only, which disappears from the built JavaScript. Your project's TypeScript settings ask for it, so the build never tries to import something that exists only for type checking. When another feature needs `ProductCard` one day, you add one line here, and that line is the moment to decide whether it should be shared at all.

examples.prompt: A checkout page imports `ProductCard` from inside the products folder, past its `index.ts`. Running the linter catches it.

examples.explanation:
oxlint reports one error, points at the line, underlines the import, and prints the rule's `message` as help. The command exits with an error too, so an automatic check that runs before code is merged would stop it.

The fix is a decision, not a different path. If checkout really needs a product card, export `ProductCard` from `@/features/products/index.ts`, or move it to `components/ui` if every feature needs it. Either way, the choice is made once, in plain sight, instead of in a stray import nobody notices.

recap:
- A single-page app changes the address with pushState and renders the matching components, so no new HTML is requested.
- The server must answer every app address with index.html, or shared links to inner pages fail with 404.
- Routes nest: each layout route renders its matching child at its Outlet, so the shared frame is written once.
- Link and NavLink navigate without a reload, and NavLink marks the current page with aria-current.
- Params and search params put what a screen shows in the address, where it survives reloads and Back works.
- Loaders fetch before a page renders, all at once, and actions handle forms, then the page's loaders run again.
- Error boundaries catch thrown errors per route, lazy routes split code, and middleware guards logged-in pages.
- Group files by feature, give each feature an index.ts, and let the linter keep imports flowing one way.
